module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Ben Green's Open Problem 3

*References:*
- [Ben Green's Open Problem 3](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#section.3 Problem 3)
- [FGY26] Franchi, Leonardo and Gowers, W. T. and Yip, Fredy, *Product-free subsets of $(0,1)$*,
  [arXiv:2607.06073](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06073), Theorem 1.1.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Set MeasureTheory

namespace Green3

/-- Suppose that $A \subset [0,1]$ is open and has measure greater than $\frac{1}{3}$. Is there a
solution to $xy = z$ with $x, y, z \in A$?

The answer is yes. [FGY26] prove that an open product-free subset of $(0,1)$ has measure strictly
less than $\frac{1}{3}$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem green_3 :
    answer(True) ↔ ∀ A : Set ℝ,
      IsOpen A → A ⊆ Icc 0 1 → volume A > 1/3 →
        ∃ x y z, x ∈ A ∧ y ∈ A ∧ z ∈ A ∧ x * y = z := by
  sorry

end Green3

findings.description: The module docstring links to the source as `https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#section.3 Problem 3`. In Green's PDF the named destination `section.3` is chapter 3, "Sumsets and bases", not Problem 3. Problem 3 is in chapter 1, "Sum-free sets, product-free sets". The anchor looks like it used the problem number instead of the chapter number, which is what other Green files use (e.g. `7.lean` uses `#section.1`, `61.lean` uses `#section.8`). The link therefore opens the wrong part of the source. The mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: In the PDF outline, `/D (section.3)` has the title "3. Sumsets and bases", while the text "Problem 3. Suppose that A ⊂ [0,1] is open and has measure greater than 1/3. Is there a solution to xy = z?" appears under "1. Sum-free sets, product-free sets". The PDF's names tree also has a `(problem.3)` destination. Source: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf
findings.suggested_fix: Use `[Ben Green's Open Problem 3](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.3)`, as `GreensOpenProblems/72.lean` does with `#problem.72`, or else `#section.1`.

reformulations.difference: The Lean requires `IsOpen A` in ℝ together with `A ⊆ Icc 0 1`, which forces A ⊆ (0,1). Green writes "A ⊂ [0,1] is open", which can be read as relatively open in [0,1], so A could contain 0 or 1. FGY26 state the problem for open subsets of the open interval (0,1). The Lean also writes out "with x, y, z ∈ A", which Green leaves implicit, and it allows x = y.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) If A is open in ℝ and A ⊆ [0,1], then A ⊆ interior[0,1] = (0,1). (2) A relatively open A = U ∩ [0,1], with U open, either contains 0 or 1, giving the trivial solutions 0·0 = 0 or 1·1 = 1, or equals U ∩ (0,1). That set is open in ℝ, lies in [0,1] and has the same measure. So the universal statement over sets open in ℝ is equivalent to the one over relatively open sets. (3) Distinctness does not matter either. For open A ⊆ (0,1), a solution x·y = z in A can be perturbed: replace y by some t ≠ x, y near y with t ∈ A and x·t ∈ A. Since 0 < x, t < 1, x·t is below both, so the three are pairwise distinct. So a 'nontrivial solution' reading poses the same problem.

review.notes: The file has one theorem, `Green3.green_3`, and it faithfully states Green's Problem 3. The elaborated statement uses Lebesgue `volume` on ℝ, the standard topology, `(1:ℝ≥0∞)/3`, which I proved equal to `ENNReal.ofReal (1/3)`, and real x, y, z. The hypotheses can be satisfied, e.g. by (0,1). The statement is not trivially provable: FGY26 note that the easy bound is 1/2 and that elementary improvements reach only about 0.3415. `answer(True)` together with `research solved` agrees with FGY26 Theorem 1.1 ('open product-free subset of (0,1) has |A| < 1/3'). The paper's line 791 also says 'at most 1/3'; either form settles Green's '> 1/3' question affirmatively. Green's own list (PDF dated 2026-01-30) still shows Problem 3 as open because it predates FGY26 (July 2026). The file cites FGY26 for the solution, so its status is consistent with the literature and there is no status issue. I did not check the 53-page proof itself; it is by established authors and the file only records it as solved. The only finding is a minor reference-anchor slip (`#section.3` points to chapter 3 instead of Problem 3). The Lean facts were compiled in /workspace/review/scratch.lean and scratch2.lean: the `1/3` identity, satisfiability of the hypotheses, open ⊆ [0,1] implies ⊆ (0,1), equivalence with the relatively-open reading, and the reduction to pairwise-distinct solutions.
